title: #19 Ask me two questions
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Craig Barton traces the evolution of his end-of-explanation questioning technique over twelve years, from the ineffective "Does anybody have any questions?" (met with silence and opt-out) to "Ask me a question" (a command that increased engagement) to his current practice of "Ask me two questions." He argues that requiring two questions rather than one pushes students past the first, most obvious question and surfaces genuinely useful gaps in understanding. He lays out a three-step routine he calls the "Holy Trinity of Participation": students write two questions individually on mini-whiteboards, then compare with a partner, then the teacher Warm Calls (a variant of Cold Call where the teacher already has a sense of the answer) students to share. The piece is a compact case study in how a small linguistic tweak, from question to command, changes participation rates, framed as an invitation for readers to try the technique themselves.
points: Reframing "Does anybody have any questions?" as a command ("Ask me a question") measurably increased student engagement because it closed off the easy opt-out of staying silent.
Asking for two questions instead of one forces students past the "same one or two questions from all students" and surfaces less obvious gaps in understanding.

The "Holy Trinity of Participation" sequence, individual mini-whiteboard writing, then paired comparison, then Warm Call, builds in accountability and gives the teacher multiple checkpoints before choosing who to call on.

Warm Calling (targeting a student the teacher already suspects has something useful to share, unlike blind Cold Call) lets the teacher pick strategically based on what was observed during circulation.
quotes: The problem is this was often met by a wall of silence (which I often interpreted as a signal of understanding), or at best a response from one or two of the more confident students.
The problem with Does anybody have any questions? is that it is too easy to opt-out.
The fact that this was now a command instead of an inquiry meant more students were willing to engage.
Asking for just one question usually results in the same one or two questions from all students.
But asking for another question really gets the students thinking and can reveal an aspect of your explanation, worked example or set of solutions that might otherwise have gone unnoticed.
Students think of their two questions on their own and write them down on their mini-whiteboards.

I then Warm Call students (Warm Call is just the same as Cold Call, but you have a sense of what students are going to say before you ask them) to share their questions based on my initial check of mini-whiteboards and what I have learned during circulation.
